## **Mastering Bone Graft Fundamentals:**
A Medical Educator’s Approach to Biologics Training


While Haleigh described what training looks like in the field, JJ Grandusky explained how that confidence is built.


JJ’s perspective is shaped by a career that includes time as a scrub technician, sales representative, and educator. Early in his sales career, he attended a biologics training that still influences how he thinks about grafts and bone healing today.


**“The core principles don’t change.”**


For JJ, effective education starts with fundamentals.


Those principles include understanding bone healing, bone biology, the three “O’s” (osteoconduction, osteoinductivity, and osteogenicity), and how patients respond after receiving a graft. Once representatives understand that foundation, they are better equipped to evaluate evolving technologies and assess the science behind them.


Rather than memorizing product features, JJ believes representatives should understand the “why” behind the technology.


When preparing for surgeon conversations, he encourages representatives to focus on understanding the clinical challenges surgeons are seeking to address.


That approach requires understanding the procedure, the surgeon’s goals, the patient population, and the outcome everyone is working toward.


Clinical evidence also plays an important role.


**“You’ve got to know them; you’ve got to know the data.”**


For JJ, studies should inform conversations, not replace them. Representatives should understand the evidence well enough to discuss it confidently while continuing to engage surgeons with thoughtful questions and meaningful follow-up.


He also believes that relationships alone are not enough to create exceptional representatives.


**“A really great rep is regularly challenging their surgeons and helping them treat their patients in a new and different way time and time again.”**


Developing that capability requires ongoing learning and practice.


**“I firmly believe this. Sales reps do not practice enough.”**


JJ compared sales preparation to athletic training. Athletes spend the majority of their time practicing before they perform. Representatives, on the other hand, often spend most of their time performing and relatively little time rehearsing conversations, objections, or clinical discussions.


More opportunities to practice can help bridge that gap and improve confidence.


As he summarized:


> Great reps are out there, and a lot of them are in the bodies of good reps right now. We can help them be great.
